planting.note: Divide and replant in early spring just as new growth begins, or in early fall.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, though established clumps handle drier shade and root competition from trees better than most epimediums once settled in. This naturally occurring hybrid of E. alpinum and E. pubigerum first arose at Cambridge Botanic Garden and is prized as one of the toughest, most vigorous barrenworts for difficult sites, spreading steadily by rhizomes into a dense evergreen carpet. Airy sprays of small, pale sulfur-yellow flowers with a coppery blush rise just above the leathery, spiny-edged foliage in mid to late spring. Shear or comb out tattered winter leaves before new growth emerges to show the flowers to best advantage.

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall; foliage stays evergreen in mild winters but may need a spring cleanup north of zone 7.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this Honshu, Japan native forms tidy clumping mounds of shield-shaped, red-tinged leaflets rather than running aggressively, making it useful for smaller woodland plantings. Large, long-spurred flowers open in mid spring in shades from white to soft violet-purple, held clear of the foliage on wiry stems, and it has served as an important parent in many garden hybrids valued for large flower size. Foliage is truly evergreen in mild-winter climates but may go semi-deciduous where winters are harsh, so tidy up worn leaves before bloom to display the flowers cleanly.

planting.note: A slower-establishing dwarf species; keep newly divided crowns consistently moist through their first season.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil in dappled to full shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind. Collected from the Erlang Shan area of Sichuan and still uncommon in gardens, this dwarf, nearly leathery-leaved species carries unusually large, bright sulfur-yellow flowers relative to its compact stature, opening on short stalks close above the evergreen foliage in spring. Its low, tidy habit and bold flower color suit a shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland border where its diminutive size would otherwise be lost among larger epimediums. Mulch with leaf mold annually to maintain the humus-rich conditions it needs and divide only when clumps become congested, since it resents frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall; tolerates a wider pH and moisture range than many epimediums.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; arrow-leaf epimedium is a Chinese species named for its narrow, arrow-shaped leaflets with pronounced basal lobes, forming a taller, more upright clump than many barrenworts. Loose sprays of small white flowers with short spurs appear above the foliage in late spring, followed by evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves that persist as useful winter groundcover in milder climates. Long grown in China as a source of the traditional herb yin yang huo, it is equally valued in the ornamental garden for its distinctive foliage texture and reliable performance in dry shade beneath trees. Established plants are drought-tolerant and require little maintenance beyond an annual tidy of old foliage before spring growth resumes.
